name: Winston Churchill
tagline: A weak pupil who taught himself, then refused to give in when Britain stood alone.
startedFrom: He was born in 1874 at Blenheim Palace into a rich aristocratic family, the son of Lord Randolph Churchill and his American wife Jennie Jerome. He wrote that he loved his mother 'at a distance' and that his nurse, Mrs Everest, was the one he confided in. He did badly at school, spent about a year in the lowest form at Harrow, and got into Sandhurst on his third try, and then only for the cavalry.

evidence.claim: At Harrow in October 1941 he told the boys the lesson of the past year was never to give in except to convictions of honour and good sense.
On 4 June 1940, after Dunkirk, he told the Commons: we shall never surrender.
When the War Cabinet met nine times from 26 to 28 May 1940, he argued against Lord Halifax's plan to explore peace terms through Mussolini, and on 28 May turned the French proposal down.
The New York Times obituary quotes Harold Macmillan: the other side of his exhausting obstinacy was undefeatable determination.
Taken prisoner by the Boers in November 1899, he climbed the wall of his Pretoria prison at the one moment the sentries could not see its top, and escaped; his comrade failed to follow.
evidence.locator: ch. III 'The Bright Eyes of Danger', pp. 48-49

evidence.claim: He wrote that on 12 December 1899 he pulled himself up the wall twice, let himself down in sickly hesitation, and went over at the third try.
evidence.locator: ch. XXI 'I Escape from the Boers - I', pp. 283-284

evidence.claim: After resigning over Gallipoli in 1915 he went to the Western Front to fight himself.
evidence.locator: Past Prime Ministers: Winston Churchill, biography

evidence.claim: The Swedish Academy's 1953 presentation speech calls him the man who has himself been through the fire, taken risks and withstood extreme pressure.
evidence.locator: presentation speech, paragraph on the First World War

evidence.claim: In 1899 he planned to leave the army, live by his books and journalism, and look for a chance to enter Parliament; he wrote that these plans were mostly carried out.
evidence.locator: ch. XVI 'I Leave the Army', pp. 213-214

evidence.claim: He was elected Conservative MP for Oldham in 1900, at 25, crossed to the Liberals in 1904, and climbed the ranks of the Liberal government over the next decade.
evidence.locator: Past Prime Ministers: Winston Churchill, biography

evidence.claim: His 1905 biographer wrote that he did not hide his ambition and that a passion to lead and to excel showed in everything he wrote.
He wrote that only in the winter of 1896, aged nearly 22, did the desire for learning come upon him.
As a cavalry officer in Bangalore he had books sent out every month and read all eight volumes of Gibbon's Decline and Fall in the midday heat, then Macaulay.
The Swedish Academy's presentation speech says he never studied at Oxford and had to spend his leisure hours educating himself.
evidence.locator: presentation speech, paragraph on Great Contemporaries

evidence.claim: In a letter thanking his mother for the books she sent, he said he was reading 50 pages of Macaulay and 25 of Gibbon every day.
evidence.locator: article citing R. S. Churchill (ed.), The Churchill Documents, vol. 2, p. 730 (footnote 8)

evidence.claim: Writing The River War in 1899 he worked at style, copying Macaulay and Gibbon, and decided the paragraph mattered as much as the sentence.
evidence.locator: ch. XVI 'I Leave the Army', p. 225

evidence.claim: He won the 1953 Nobel Prize in Literature for his mastery of historical and biographical description and for brilliant oratory.
Over 60 years in the House of Commons he found time to write more than two dozen books.

principles.text: Never give in, unless honour and good sense tell you to.
Tell people the hard truth about what is coming; do not promise an easy road.
If your schooling left gaps, fill them yourself by reading the great books.
Use your young years to act now; do not settle for things as they are.

quotes.text: I have nothing to offer but blood, toil, tears and sweat.
We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields and in the streets, we shall fight in the hills; we shall never surrender
Never give in, never give in, never, never, never—in nothing, great or small, large or petty—never give in except to convictions of honour and good sense.
Twenty to twenty-five! These are the years! Don't be content with things as they are.

definingMoment.text: In late May 1940, with the British army trapped around Dunkirk, Foreign Secretary Lord Halifax pressed the War Cabinet to explore peace terms through Mussolini. The War Cabinet met nine times from 26 to 28 May and Churchill argued against it; the minutes record him saying that nations which went down fighting rose again, but those which surrendered tamely were finished. On 28 May he told about twenty-five ministers outside the War Cabinet that Britain would fight on, and they backed him. That night he turned down the French proposal, and on 4 June he told the Commons that Britain would never surrender.

shadow.text: He fought Indian self-rule through the 1930s; in a speech on 23 February 1931 he described Gandhi 'striding half-naked up the steps of the Vice-regal palace'. He said 'The Aryan stock is bound to triumph' in 1901 and spoke of 'a higher grade race' to the Peel Commission on Palestine in 1937, as his defender Richard Langworth confirms. In a War Office minute of 12 May 1919 he wrote 'I am strongly in favour of using poisoned gas against uncivilised tribes'; the same minute names lachrymatory gas, and Langworth says he meant tear gas. In 1943, while he led the War Cabinet, famine in Bengal killed up to three million people. Madhusree Mukerjee's 2010 book argues that he had food sent away from starving Indians and reports him blaming the famine on Indians 'breeding like rabbits'; historian Janam Mukherjee says he played a role in blocking imports but that blaming him alone is 'highly misleading'; and defenders Arthur Herman and Richard Langworth say the ships could not be spared and credit his choice of Wavell as Viceroy with easing the famine.

councilQuestion.text: What did you give up on this week that honour and good sense did not ask you to drop?

screen.notes: Real British prime minister who died in 1965, so not a living politician or founder of a religion; no credible account of sexual violence or of sexual contact with anyone under 16 was found; he has a documented dark side on race, India and the 1943 Bengal famine.

review.devilsAdvocate: I attacked all five values and re-read every locator in My Early Life (1930), Scott (1905), Hansard, the Harrow transcript, the Nobel pages, the Museum of the Prime Minister and the shadow sources. Nothing fell: Determination, Courage and Ambition matched the blind pick, Learning reached three sources with a Hillsdale-cited letter, and Craft held despite David Reynolds showing his war memoirs were largely drafted by assistants, since his early books and speeches were his own. Two claims overstated their sources (he did not climb the Pretoria wall in sight of the sentries, and the nine May 1940 meetings were the War Cabinet's, not nine of his arguments) and are fixed. The shadow gained his own 12 May 1919 minute on poison gas, with Langworth's tear-gas reading beside it.
